📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced set of slo-mo videos gives us a new perspective on SpaceX's first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage.

The company notched the milestone on Saturday (Nov. 14), when the launch tower at its Starbase site in South Texas caught Starship's Ship spacecraft with its "chopstick" arms.

You've probably seen photos and videos showing the epic snag from afar. But on Tuesday (Nov. 17), SpaceX released up-close views — a series of four slo-mo videos captured by cameras near the top of the 480-foot-tall (146 meters) tower.

According to recent reports, "The Starbase tower chopsticks catching their first Starship. This unique architecture was designed for full and rapid reusability, enabling repeat debuts and landings from the same pad," SpaceX wrote in a Tuesday X post that shared the videos, a compilation of which you can see embedded above.

Recent findings suggest that starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. Its current "V3" version stands about 408 feet (124 m) tall, and future iterations will be even larger.

Industry observers note that as SpaceX noted in Tuesday's post, the megarocket is also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first for an orbital launch system. The company plans to catch both Starship stages — Ship and the Super Heavy booster — at the launch tower, a recovery strategy designed to enable efficient inspection, refurbishment and reflight.

SpaceX planned to carry out such a double catch on this most recent test flight, Starship's 15th to date, which debuted on Friday evening (Nov. 13). But Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel warning during its return to Starbase about 6.5 minutes after launch and autonomously diverted to splash down in the Gulf of Mexico.

In a recent development, that wasn't a huge deal for SpaceX, as it had already caught Super Heavy on three previous test flights. Snagging Ship is tougher; the upper stage returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter than the booster does.

SpaceX had not even attempted a Ship catch before Flight 15. But the manufacturer managed to pull off the maneuver on its first try.

And Ship did some work in orbit before coming home: It deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites on Flight 15, the second batch that the company has sent to low Earth orbit. The first set was deployed on Flight 14, which introduced on Sept. 28.

Industry observers note that discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

In a recent development, explanation: Today's image could have been a painting. But what do these colors mean? The brightest star, left of the center, is blue Alnitak (the Girdle): a triple star system best known for being the easternmost star in Orion's Belt. The instantly recognizable shape of a dark horse's head at the center is the aptly named Horsehead Nebula. It is about five light-years tall and lies approximately 1,500 light-years away. It is made of dust and gas that obscure the red glow behind it, which is caused by hydrogen gas being ionized by the bright star Sigma Orionis at the top. The orange nebula with dark filaments on the left is the Flame Nebula. Closer to the Horsehead, the blue reflection nebula NGC 2023 is actively forming stars. The data for this "painting" were collected for almost six hours at the Utah Desert Remote Observatories, but the equipment was remotely controlled by the astrophotographer from his home, over 2,000 km away in Illinois.Tomorrow's picture: V-G-R.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the world’s largest energy shock in history and growing climate change concerns this year are reshaping the future of how people will power homes, drive cars and fuel industries, according to an International Energy Agency report released Thursday.The energy crisis, triggered by the Iran war, will “leave lasting marks” on the world’s energy sector, according to the Paris-based IEA, founded after the 1973-74 energy crisis.Energy-hungry nations will prioritize the security and affordability of their electricity, the report remarked. This is a boon for renewable technologies, like solar, and alternative technologies, like nuclear. But it is also reinforcing the case to keep coal as a backup in times of crisis.This is especially true in coal-rich Asia, which went into energy triage when the Iran war cut off the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway where around a fifth of the world’s traded oil typically flows.The report looks “past the current turmoil to explore the range of energy futures that could emerge from today’s upheaval,” said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol. He said the Iran war “delivered a huge shock to the system” and warned “the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be.”“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” he said.Annual United Nations climate talks, known as COP31 and hosted in Turkey this year, are in their second and final week. Before these negotiations, the U.N. announced the world is dangerously close to missing its goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.Electrification — the process of powering homes, cars and industries with electricity — and moving away from planet-warming fossil fuels are the two substantial ticket issues at this year’s climate talks.“The future of the energy system and our climate are inextricably intertwined,” said Rachel Cleetus, climate program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at COP31. Flagship report forecasts energy future The IEA, the world’s leading intergovernmental energy organization with more than 30 member countries, publishes World Energy Outlooks annually.This year’s 560-page plus report analyzes government and private data to project various future scenarios based on whether countries will continue with current policies or drastically change policies in the face of ongoing crises.The world’s energy sector will clearly have a before and after the Iran war, experts said. In March, the IEA coordinated the emergency release of 400 million barrels of crude oil stocks to stabilize global markets.“This crisis has exposed the price of fossil fuel dependence,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. “It’s crazy that a conflict thousands of miles away can send energy bills soaring at home.”Conflicts, trade tensions, climate risks and cyberattacks are increasing the number of possible energy futures. The IEA said the “drive to diversify” fuel supplies will reshape the energy trade.The Middle East will still be the world’s largest oil exporter, but nations will likely reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. The IEA forecasts the amount of oil transiting the strait could go from 20 million barrels per day before the Iran war, to 8.5 million barrels in 2030, and even under 2 million barrels by 2035.While fossil fuels still dominate national energy mixes, the IEA said renewables — led by solar — and nuclear power are the “biggest beneficiaries” of governments trying to grow domestic energy sources. But energy security concerns may lead coal-rich nations to rely on the fossil fuel as a fallback option during times of crisis.“When we look at how energy crises change the world over the long term, governments are only just beginning to get their head around just how much things will change,” said Dave Jones, co-founder of the think tank Ember. Climate talks eye electrification The ongoing talks in Turkey follow a year rattled by the Iran war’s energy shock, as well as several climate-induced disasters.Global warming adds pressure to rising electricity demand. In what the IEA called a “striking milestone,” energy demand for cooling is overtaking energy demand for heating for the first time.India, the world’s most populous nation, will account for more energy demand growth over the next decade than any other country or region. China, already one of the world’s most electrified economies, may see its electrification grow from 32% last year to 43% by 2035 — the highest among any major economy.At COP31, Turkey is pushing for the world to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035.While the preference would be for this to come from renewable energy, U.N. documents on the negotiating table don’t spell this out. That means coal and other fossil fuels could be used, at least initially.“The IEA’s latest report makes clear that the fossil energy crisis unleashed by the US-Israel war on Iran has irrevocably changed the global energy system, adding to the many reasons why countries would benefit from a rapid transition to clean energy and electrification,” said Cleetus, with the Union of Concerned Scientists. The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. The AP is solely responsible for all content. Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.
  • Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.
  • In a recent development, confirmed Thursday, its newly introduced “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.

Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.

In a recent development, confirmed Thursday, its newly introduced “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.

In a recent development, nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN. The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.

Recent findings suggest that nectar claims its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.

Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds latest matches as creators become more popular.

Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.

Recent findings suggest that “Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being remarked in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.”.

Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a fresh baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals.

Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers.

The firm plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents.

This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that intel has reduced its workforce by approximately 27,800 employees under Lip-Bu Tan, based on the organization's reported headcount figures, but this does not seem to be enough.
  • It has been revealed that the latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech.
  • It has been revealed that the latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that intel has reduced its workforce by approximately 27,800 employees under Lip-Bu Tan, based on the organization's reported headcount figures, but this does not seem to be enough. The company has reportedly initiated another round of layoffs, this time across its global information technology (IT) organization, as its chief executive continues to reduce expenses and simplify the company's operations, reports Business Insider.

It has been revealed that the latest cuts in Intel's IT organization reportedly began on November 16, although Intel has not disclosed how many employees will lose their jobs, notes TrendForce citing CTech. Some employees claim that the reductions could affect a double-digit percentage of the department's workforce of around 2,607 people at 55 sites in 53 countries, so we are talking about at least 260 people if we are talking about a 10% reduction, or as much as 520 if we are talking about a 20% reduction. One has to keep in mind that these estimates have not been independently verified. Intel has neither confirmed the number of affected employees nor identified the specific teams involved. Instead, the company reiterated to Business Insider that it regularly reviews its workforce to ensure that personnel and financial resources correspond to its strategic priorities.

It has been revealed that the latest reductions follow several rounds of layoffs throughout 2026. In July, Intel eliminated positions in its Data Center and AI Group. Between July and October, the manufacturer submitted nine Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) notices in California, which covered 222 employees, according to Business Insider. The most recent notice, filed on October 22, concerned 67 permanent job cuts at Intel's Folsom campus (which mostly specializes in R&D, hardware validation, and software development), effective October 31. As of November 17, no additional WARN notices had been reported.

According to recent reports, intel employed 81,100 people as of September 27, 2026, including 76,500 employees at Intel itself and another 4,600 at Mobileye and other subsidiaries. This compares with 85,100 employees at the end of 2025 and 108,900 a year earlier, which means that the organization's workforce declined by 4,000 since December, 2025, and 27,800 since December, 2024. respectively.

According to recent reports, intel's workforce reductions began well before Lip-Bu Tan became chief executive in 2025. In 2024, his predecessor Pat Gelsinger announced looks to eliminate more than 15,000 positions, or approximately 15% of the company’s workforce. Tan has continued to reduce expenses, eliminate management layers, and discontinue lower-priority projects as Intel attempts to cut costs and reduce losses/improve profitability.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the firm confirmed on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

In a recent development, with its open source roots, the startup claims its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock owners into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including substantial-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (464 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For anyone who has ever hit share, only to spot a typo moments later, Instagram now has a fix for that.
  • According to recent reports, for anyone who has ever hit share, only to spot a typo moments later, Instagram now has a fix for that.
  • Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed the upcoming feature Wednesday in a post on his Instagram feed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For anyone who has ever hit share, only to spot a typo moments later, Instagram now has a fix for that. The Meta-owned platform is rolling out a feature that lets you edit a story after you post it. Instagram head Adam Mosseri declared the new feature Wednesday in a post on his Instagram feed. “A lot of people have been asking for this, so I’m excited to get this one out there,” he shared in the post. You can edit text, music, stickers, and drawings, but there’s one catch: you have to act fast. You can only make edits to a story within 15 minutes of sharing. You can fix typos and other mistakes without losing your views, likes, or replies. Previously, the only option besides leaving the story up was to delete it and repost. A few other details worth knowing  When you edit a story, Instagram adds an edited label, and your audience stays the same. Any previous reshares of the story get removed. According to Instagram, editing is not available on stories that were also shared to Facebook or contain certain stickers. How to edit an Instagram story: Open your published story. Tap the three dots “More” button. Select Edit story. Fix your text, or patch stickers, drawing, or music. Save the changes. Instagram announced the feature along with other stories upgrades, including new sticker designs, an easier way to select multiple photos, and backgrounds for photos of any size.

I’ve Been a CFO, a CPA, a Franchisee and a CEO — Here Are the Credentials That Get You Hired Now

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Industry observers note that I’ve had a lot of impressive titles.
  • It has been revealed that early in my career, I believed my credentials did the talking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that I’ve had a lot of impressive titles. But titles describe what you’ve already done. In today’s AI-driven market, decision-makers want proof of how you think, who will vouch for you and what you’ll do next.

It has been revealed that early in my career, I believed my credentials did the talking. I became a CPA with a global Big 6 firm and then worked my way into CFO and CEO roles. Later, I became a franchise business owner and learned more about grit, determination and humility than I had in the previous 20 years combined.

In a recent development, each of those titles opened a door at one point. None of them, on their own, would get me hired today.

In a recent development, I see this play out every week. As a franchise consultant, I spend most of my time with directors, vice presidents and CXOs, many of them facing a restructuring. Their resumes are stacked. Yet the ones who land on their feet fastest, whether that means a newly introduced role, a board seat or a franchise award, rarely win on titles. They win on a different set of credentials, and some of those can be built in months, not decades.

Here are the four I’ve seen matter most.

According to recent reports, A title indicates you held a job. A point of view indicates how you thought while you held it. When I was a CFO at a real estate developer, my work was buried in spreadsheets and board meetings. Nobody outside the building knew how I approached the cash crunch during the Great Recession or difficult acquisitions.

According to recent reports, when I started my national consulting firm, I had no choice but to put my thinking in public. I began posting regularly on LinkedIn about franchise ownership, career transitions and the lessons learned as a franchisee. That consistency, more than any credential on my profile, is why strangers started calling. More than 20,000 people now follow me, and many executives tell me they read my posts long before reaching out to me.

Pick two or three topics where your experience gives you a unique viewpoint and write about them every week. You aren’t building an audience for its own sake. You’re creating a searchable record of your expertise.

Earlier in my career, my network was mostly people I’d worked with directly. That works until you’re in transition or need help outside your industry, which is exactly when most people need it. I learned this through three reorganizations. Three of the four companies I worked for over 26 years no longer exist. So I started nurturing my network long before I needed it.

Franchisors taught me this lesson from the other side of the table. When candidates apply to buy a franchise, the franchisor evaluates them just as carefully as the candidate evaluates the brand. The candidates who move through smoothly are the ones other people will vouch for — former colleagues, bankers and existing owners in the system.

In a recent development, this is where LinkedIn Premium has earned a spot in my toolkit. I use Sales Navigator to find and follow the executives I serve and to identify mutual connections who could make a warm introduction. I don’t use it to blast messages. I use it to find a valued connection who can vouch for me, and then I ask that person directly.

Sources indicate that think of 25 people who will take your call tomorrow. If fewer than half of them work outside your current tech giant, start widening the circle now, while you don’t need favors. And never send a message that doesn’t offer the other person something of value.

This credential surprises executives the most. As a CEO, I had people build the model, chase the receivables and fix the website. As a fitness franchise owner, I was the OEO — the Only Executive Officer — and I tell my candidates to expect the same.

Hiring managers and franchisors are asking a version of the same question: Will this person roll up their sleeves and do the work, not just direct it? You answer that with evidence. Maybe you’ve run a side project, advised a small business or built your own department or systems.

Sources indicate that today I run a national practice largely on my own. The tools I pay for earn their keep only because they let one person do the work a small team used to do.

Identify one hands-on accomplishment from the past two years that didn’t depend on a team and make it visible.

It has been revealed that the fastest way to look obsolete is to describe how things were done a decade ago. The old adage “if it isn’t broken, don’t fix it” doesn’t apply today. The executives I see winning today are adaptable. One of my candidates just bought a second franchise in a different industry because she has an insatiable appetite for learning.

After more than 30 years in business, I’m still learning. I’m working on a second edition of my book because some of my original advice needs updating. Admitting that isn’t a weakness. It tells people I’m paying attention.

Be ready to explain, in two sentences, something you’ve learned in the past six months and how you’ve applied it. I’m not dismissing traditional credentials. My CPA background is the reason candidates trust me to walk them through financing options. My years as a CFO and CEO gave me pattern recognition no course could teach.

Sources indicate that but titles are only a starting point. They tell people what you’ve done. The four points above tell them what you’ll do next.

Start this week. Write one post that shares a real lesson from your career. Reach out to three people outside your organization. Add something to your profile that you built, not just something you managed. Those small moves compound faster than you’d expect.

In a recent development, if you want a head start, LinkedIn’s Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to find the ones that fit the way you work.

According to recent reports, each of those titles opened a door at one point. None of them, on their own, would get me hired today.

#92. Jensen Huang’s departure blasts major hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say

Jensen Huang’s departure blasts major hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the resignation heard across the world.
  • Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook.
  • Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the organization for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a major blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.

According to recent reports, most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.

Recent findings suggest that “She’s much more conservative,” one investor stated of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”.

According to recent reports, nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a substantial reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.

In a recent development, for instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.

“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya mentioned of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”.

It has been revealed that it’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

Industry observers note that if the organization does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google revealed two latest chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.).

Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

Sources indicate that dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Major Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he noted. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

Sources indicate that under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.

Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the newly introduced companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.

Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

In a recent development, though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, mentioned that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”.

#91. NASA’s Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1008 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nasa ↗ Open Full Page

NASA’s Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel.
  • Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday.
  • “Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18.

Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday.

“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” stated Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.”.

Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Sources indicate that even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data.

Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, released in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances.

“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward latest frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”.

In addition to their suite of scientific instruments, the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it.

Sources indicate that “Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” mentioned Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.”.

Traveling about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), Voyager 1 in 2012 became the first spacecraft to leave the heliosphere, the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun that deflects cosmic radiation, and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2, taking a different trajectory, crossed the boundary in 2018.

According to recent reports, “The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” stated Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One substantial surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.”.

Creative engineering solutions have enabled the probes to conserve energy and overcome challenges related to aging hardware, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer on the spacecraft. Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives — a move not without risk — to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator. Essentially a nuclear battery, the generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity.

In a recent development, with the plutonium supply continually depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer.

As with all NASA spacecraft that venture to and beyond the Moon, communication between Earth and the Voyager probes is managed by the agency’s Deep Space Network, large antennas located at three facilities around the world.

It has been revealed that “We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.”.

Tech Report: Flaming Hydra’s upcoming Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”.
  • In a recent development, that’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project, an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra.
  • To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor, Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s a big promise: A new Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”.

In a recent development, that’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project, an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra. If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a fresh e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries.

To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor, Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”.

In a recent development, bustillos told me that these issues have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself — for example, when Tal Lavin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.”.

“AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.”.

The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries.

Back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.”.

In a recent development, this is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time.

“E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.”.

In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.”.

According to recent reports, so even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a substantial deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem.

It has been revealed that flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a newly introduced, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries.

It has been revealed that the Phoenix Project is starting by offering five latest e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos stated she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model.

Similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive).

Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos said she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Ranganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent.

“We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she remarked. “Those things go hand in hand.”.

Flaming Hydra seeks to raise $30,000 for The Phoenix Project, with the campaign ending on November 27.

#88. As Power Demand Surges, Energy Is Moving Closer To The Edge

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Forbes ↗ Open Full Page

As Power Demand Surges, Energy Is Moving Closer To The Edge

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ​Over the summer, Europe suffered a heat wave that strained its power grids, simultaneously increasing electricity demand and forcing some power plants to shut down.​.
  • This isn’t the first time extreme temperatures have impacted the grid’s ability to deliver power.
  • According to recent reports, the problem is being made worse by the construction of hyperscale AI data centers, which require massive amounts of electricity and further strain the grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that darren H. S. Tan. Chief Executive Officer at UNIGRID.

​Over the summer, Europe suffered a heat wave that strained its power grids, simultaneously increasing electricity demand and forcing some power plants to shut down.​.

This isn’t the first time extreme temperatures have impacted the grid’s ability to deliver power. Many places around the world have experienced record-high or record-low temperatures in recent years, and the demand for heating or cooling reached levels that existing energy infrastructure wasn’t designed to handle. ​.

According to recent reports, the problem is being made worse by the construction of hyperscale AI data centers, which require massive amounts of electricity and further strain the grid. Completely rebuilding the grid to meet modern demands has proven fiscally impractical for many governments, forcing many places to solve the problem on the local level using distributed generation and storage.

Sources indicate that energy infrastructure across the U.S. and Europe was built over a century ago, when energy needs were much different. ​.

Industry observers note that even so, studies have shown that we use only about 40% to 55% of the grid on average, and that’s by design, so it can handle spikes when they occur. But recent extreme weather events and data center demand are causing power needs to exceed even that generous buffer.​.

Recent findings suggest that for example, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which manages electricity in Texas, has said its interconnection queue currently includes over 1,800 projects totaling 474 gigawatts of power, over five times the state’s record peak electricity demand. Ninety percent of those requests come from data centers. ​.

The cost to completely rebuild the grid to meet today’s needs is astronomical, with some estimates putting the total replacement cost in the trillions. Because of the potential cost and the fact that the aging grid is a chronic rather than an urgent problem, it receives patchwork upgrades as needed and as government budgets allow. ​.

With a full rebuild out of the picture, several strategies are in play to work within the system we already have. When demand approaches available supply, energy companies offer rebates for reducing usage at peak times, implement peak pricing or, in more extreme cases, resort to rolling blackouts, which are planned outages to alleviate the demand during peak periods. ​.

Beyond the grid itself, some areas are reducing their dependence on the centralized infrastructure by moving toward local power generation and storage.

Battery energy storage systems (BESS) can store electricity and discharge it when demand exceeds the grid’s capacity. ​.

They are already showing promise in several states, such as California, where battery storage capacity has reached over 21,000 MW, equal to about one-third of the state’s peak demand. Eighty percent of that capacity is represented by grid-connected batteries, but smaller batteries are also enabling residents to increase their own energy storage capacity at home.​.

As these batteries become cheaper and more reliable, it’s not out of the realm of possibility that these energy storage systems become a standard household appliance in the future, much like a refrigerator or washing machine is today. They can also play a role in energy needs for small businesses.

Being able to store energy and use it in an emergency is only half the equation. The other half is being able to generate electricity independently of the grid. ​.

According to recent reports, this isn’t a concept that should be unfamiliar to many, as many organizations and homes already have backup generators or solar panels. Although these methods can keep small businesses and homes powered up, they have their disadvantages. Generators are noisy, pollutive and can be dangerous, while solar has significant upfront installation costs. ​.

According to recent reports, plug-in solar is emerging as another option for generating electricity locally that has already seen success in Europe and is starting to gain support in the U.S. as well. Instead of being installed on a rooftop, these smaller panels can be mounted on a balcony or a small section of a yard or business property and plugged into a wall outlet to help power homes and small businesses. ​.

It has been revealed that these systems cost significantly less than traditional solar and are portable, so people can move them around wherever they’re needed. These benefits open up power generation to a whole fresh segment of the country: commercial and residential renters alike who might never invest in a hardwired battery system or solar installation.

As energy demand continues to increase, expanding traditional grid infrastructure will remain vital, but those projects can be expensive and take years to complete. Distributed generation and storage offer another way to increase resilience in the meantime. ​.

By generating and storing more electricity closer to where it will be consumed, communities and business leaders can help reduce their reliance on the centralized grid during peak demand.​.

We’re unlikely to solve growing power constraints with any single technology, but as local generation and storage become cheaper and more accessible, they can play a larger role in managing peak demand and making better use of the grid infrastructure we already have.​.

Tech Report: Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a fresh social simulator powered by AI.
  • MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a newly introduced social simulator powered by AI.
  • Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims, is working on a new game — and it’s built around AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a fresh social simulator powered by AI.

MyMems, from the creator of SimCity and The Sims, is a newly introduced social simulator powered by AI.

Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims, is working on a new game — and it’s built around AI. The new title, focused on your memories, is called MyMems. Like Wright’s other titles, it sounds extremely ambitious, giving players a new way to explore worlds they create on their own. “We want to take your autobiography and turn it into a toy world,” he tells The Verge.

In a recent development, the MyMems website describes the mobile game as a “social simulation” with worlds “built from your memories and the people who shaped you.” You can add “memories” to your game, like speaking a short story to your phone, and those memories are generated into pieces you can place on the game’s map. Your worlds can also include AI-powered avatars, which can represent people you know in your life. Ideally, as you play, the planet starts to become a “map of your psyche,” kind of like Inside Out, Wright claims. Worlds can be private, but you can also share them with others.

Here’s another way to think of it, from Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at MyMems developer Gallium Studios: “It’s a cozy world builder with a really deep social simulation underneath.”.

In a recent development, I’ll admit that I don’t totally get it, and it seems like a tricky idea to grasp without playing it. Still, as heady of a concept as it might be — turning your memories into a game world — Wright and team still want it to be fun. “This isn’t meant to be your legacy diary necessarily,” states Anthony Maitz, a product manager at Gallium Studios. “It’s meant to just be something you kind of play around with.” However, Maitz notes that what you’re working toward is a “proxy” of you — a word that seems to be the inspiration of the game’s earlier title, Proxi: Yesterday’s You Tomorrow. The game will use the “Behavior Engine” from a company called Artificial Agency, which makes AI tech for video games, as a “foundational technology.”.

Recent findings suggest that like other industries, gaming is starting to reckon with generative AI. Early AI virtual worlds created with models from a startup backed by a Pixar cofounder and Google’s Project Genie weren’t experiences you’d actually want to spend dedicated time with, and indie developers I spoke to in March were largely opposed to the technology. But AI technology has taken some substantial leaps this year with companies like Google, Meta, and Roblox now letting consumers make games with AI right from their phone, and retro gaming becoming overrun with AI-powered ports of classic titles.

Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick remarked earlier this year that generative AI has “zero part in what Rockstar Games is building” with GTA VI. But even as a recent industry survey indicated that more game developers are starting to use generative AI as part of their job, workers are pushing back against generative AI use, and the technology is at the center of fierce debates over indie game awards.

Many players are rejecting AI outright, and I wondered if the Gallium Studios team was worried about opposition toward MyMems’ use of AI. Wright claims he has three boys at home and that they are all “pretty negative” on AI. He attributes negativity over AI to be toward the meaning of art and authorship and credit, a concern he calls “well-founded.” But he also calls AI an “amazing tool.”.

Industry observers note that “We’re not making slop,” notes McArthur. But Maitz notes that while the team has “been concerned” about a negative response to the generative AI use, they’ve learned that people don’t mind when they use AI in a “Scribblenauts-y style” for things like having the game make a high school. The team also found that people got “addicted” to a test app with a character creator, including Maitz’s own daughter, who he says “hates” AI. “By making it so that the player is authoring it over and over, bit by bit, it doesn’t really feel like you cheated,” Maitz says.

According to recent reports, myMems, which is set to launch in 2027, will join a growing field of other social simulations, like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s smash hit Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. But none quite have the pull of The Sims, which remains one of EA’s most key franchises. With The Sims, Wright says that many people tried making their real families in the game.

It has been revealed that “It was interesting how people really were naturally trying to map this game, which was like a little toy, onto their real life,” he notes. With MyMems, that’s what the team is trying to do the “follow-through” on — what if they made the whole game focused on you?

Recent findings suggest that imagine opening a family scrapbook and the way people and things jump out, Wright explains. “As you go through more and more pages, pretty soon you have this whole little circus of people and events and things from your life.” It’s chaos, he says. “I want something that feels kind of like that.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

In a recent development, the investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup claims it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology tech giant General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.

Sources indicate that the Fresh Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) stated in an interview.

“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.

Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.

Recent findings suggest that bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.

Sources indicate that the startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup looks to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.

The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indusbridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.

Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.

“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor remarked.

In 2024, Bharat Semi unveiled intends for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor stated, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.

Recent findings suggest that the project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The latest funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the AI data center build-out is pushing electricity grids across the globe, with many regions facing demand from projects that would exceed the current peak load that each system could support.
  • Industry observers note that this massive power consumption is one of the reasons for the opposition against their construction in communities, with residents blaming them for increased utility prices.
  • Emissions are another glitch that the IEA has raised.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the AI data center build-out is pushing electricity grids across the globe, with many regions facing demand from projects that would exceed the current peak load that each system could support. According to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2026 report, a total of 120GW of capacity is presently available across all types of data centers across the globe, with another 120GW expected to be completed by the end of the decade, 75% of which would be dedicated to artificial intelligence. Aside from that, it’s also tracking 93 large “AI factories” that are either under construction or being expanded via satellite imagery. It estimates that the capacity for these sites grew from under 2GW to 17GW in just two years, and that they’re expected to hit a total of 50GW upon completion, the equivalent of adding a second Great Britain to power demand.

Industry observers note that this massive power consumption is one of the reasons for the opposition against their construction in communities, with residents blaming them for increased utility prices. However, the IEA says that its analysis “does not yet show a clear relationship between growth in data center capacity and increases in electricity prices.” It noted that if a data center uses existing capacity and pays for its share of the cost, then it could potentially lead to lower utility bills for all customers. However, if the grid operator is required to upgrade its system to accommodate the large consumer, then it could also lead to increased monthly bills if the costs are spread across all users.

Emissions are another glitch that the IEA has raised. Renewable energy dominates data centers’ power purchase agreements at nearly 50%, but actual power generation puts coal- and natural-gas power sources closer to 60%. This is likely due to the need for reliability, with the latter kicking in when the former cannot deliver the power that the data center needs. Aside from that, a few projects are deploying their own power, like Elon Musk’s Colossus 2 in Southaven, Mississippi, with about 180GW planned or under construction in the U.S. So, even though renewable energy is growing to accommodate demand, it’s also expected that coal- and natural-gas emissions from data centers will rise by 70% by 2030.

Industry observers note that investments in AI data centers are expected to hit $32 trillion by 2050, putting the infrastructure spending for the industry larger than railways, electrification, and the internet, combined. Despite that, the IEA notes the grid remains a significant bottleneck — renewable power plants take between one and five years to complete, which is around the same time that some massive data center projects take if they do not face an extended moratorium, while transmission works can take three to five times longer. This is probably one of the reasons why some AI hyperscalers are choosing to put jet engines on their sites instead, although these are also facing shortages, especially in turbine blades.

Video game consoles are more expensive than ever, but sales are growing regardless, at least in the US. Circana has released its report for US video game industry sales in October, confirming that PS5 unit sales increased by 5% compared to October 2025. That's despite the average selling price of a PS5 increasing by 13%. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4FatSqS3VYY Xbox Series X|S unit sales jumped by 10% in October 2026 compared to October 2025, and the average selling price rose by 29% year-over-year. The Switch 2 was October 2026's top console in unit and dollar sales, and it remains 2026's best-performing console by those measurements, followed by PS5. However, Circana did not break out the specifics for Switch 2 unit sales or average selling price changes. Total hardware spending in the US on game consoles was up by 2%, reaching $357 million. Higher pricing drove the dollar sales growth, Circana stated, noting that PS5 dollar sales rose by 20% and Xbox Series X|S jumped by 42%. However, Switch 2 sales, measured by dollar sales, fell by 11%. Looking back to September 2026, PS5 hardware dollar sales grew by 43%, while spending on Xbox Series X|S dropped by 2% and Switch 2 fell by 12%. It will be interesting to see the November US hardware data when it comes in, as experts have said the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S could get a jolt in sales from people buying systems to play GTA 6. However, Circana has warned that sales might not be as strong as expected due to the increased prices. Microsoft, Sony, and Nintendo have raised prices on their consoles due in part to the ongoing memory and component shortages from the AI buildout. Tariffs have also played a role. On the subject of tariffs, all three received refunds from the government after the Supreme Court deemed the tariffs illegal, but those companies are keeping the money and not giving anything back to you. The companies argued that people who paid more knew what they were doing and don't deserve to get any money back.

On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid.
  • Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system.
  • It has been revealed that hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth.

Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway.

It has been revealed that hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010. Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

It has been revealed that the primary goal of Japan's Hayabusa mission to asteroid Itokawa was never to be the first spacecraft to liftoff from a space rock. The mission was always aimed at collecting samples from an asteroid and returning them to Earth.

Sources indicate that it was a hard road to Itokawa for Hayabusa. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) rolled out the probe on May 9, 2003, with aims for an arrival at the asteroid in the early summer of 2005.

That asteroid arrival was delayed until September 2005 after a solar storm degraded Hayabusa's solar arrays, limiting the available power for its ion engines.

Industry observers note that still, Hayabusa managed to limp along its path to reach the asteroid Itokawa on Sept. 12, 2005.

Hayabusa dropped a small lander onto Itokawa, but that probe was apparently lost. Hayabusa then dropped a landing target on the asteroid, and ultimately managed to touchdown about 99 feet from the marker, JAXA has said.

Recent findings suggest that during its first landing on Nov. 19, Hayabusa descended to a point just 56 feet above Itokawa before going silent for 3 hours, according to an Associated Press report. Once contact was restored, JAXA officials confirmed the probe had landed, and it eventually lifted off for a second attempt. That was the first-ever liftoff from an asteroid by a spacecraft.

Industry observers note that "The spacecraft actually bounced off the surface a few times and spent about 39 minutes resting on the asteroid, but apparently the samplers never fired," Andrew Cheng, a Hayabusa science team member at Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, told Space.com at the time. There was hope that some material managed to make it inside the collector anyway.

"After all the thrashing about ... there is no way to confirm that," Cheng had stated. The second landing on Itokawa occured a few days later on Nov. 26, 2005.

In November 2010, five months after Hayabusa's sample-return capsule touched down in Australia, JAXA declared some good news: Hayabusa did collect 1,500 dust grains from asteroid Itokawa, samples that were jammed into the collector by the two landings, despite is collector mechanism not firing.

The ultimate success of Hayabusa spurred the creation of another sample-return mission by Japan: Hayabusa2.

Recent findings suggest that that probe introduced in December 2014 and arrived at asteroid Ryugu (REE-ooh-goo) in 2018. It collected its own samples and returned them to Earth in December 2020. The Hayabusa2 probe is now on an extended mission to the asteroid 2015 BM510, which it will fly by in April 2028. It had planned to land on a strange asteroid 1998 KY26, but suffered engine trouble that made that rendezvous impossible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.
  • Recent findings suggest that the funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest.
  • In a recent development, traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.

Recent findings suggest that the funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

In a recent development, traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.

Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he noted.

That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.

At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Company Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.

Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare organization DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.

Industry observers note that the advertising sales team at media streaming tech giant Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”.

Replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.

“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he stated, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.

Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.

According to recent reports, dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows people to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.

Sources indicate that at the moment, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy mentioned the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.
